courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one upcoming change at a fictional company (for example, 'add a new regional sales report') and decide whether Waterfall, Agile, or a hybrid approach fits it, using the lesson's own criteria (how stable are the requirements, how much will people react once they see it). Then write three user stories for that change in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' format, each with one specific, checkable acceptance criterion.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph write-up naming the chosen delivery model with a one-sentence justification, plus three correctly formatted user stories with acceptance criteria.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a 5-column Kanban board (Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done) for the three user stories you wrote in the previous slot, assign a WIP limit to the In Progress column and explain in one sentence why that limit helps rather than slows the team down. Then map the same three stories through the Dev -> QA -> UAT -> Production chain, writing one sentence per stage naming who owns it and what question that stage answers.
slots.deliverable: A completed 5-column Kanban board with a stated WIP limit and reasoning, plus a one-sentence-per-stage Dev/QA/UAT/Production ownership map for the same stories.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, command by command, the Git workflow (clone, branch, commit, push, pull request) you would use to make one of the changes from Slot 1's user stories, including one properly specific commit message (not 'fixed stuff') naming what changed and why. Then build a release checklist for shipping that same change -- approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release notes -- and choose which deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) fits it best, with a one-sentence reason.
slots.deliverable: A written Git command sequence with one well-written commit message, plus a completed release checklist and a chosen deployment strategy with a stated justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the lesson's Castlebridge Retail capstone scenario end to end, using its own checklist: write user stories for the revenue-by-region view, the revenue-by-category view, and the automatic-refresh requirement, each with acceptance criteria (the refresh story must state what time the dashboard needs to reflect the prior day's sales by); build the 5-column Kanban board; write a QA test plan including the zero-sales-region edge case; write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's own voice; write short, specific release notes naming what shipped and one known limitation; then respond in writing to the simulated production incident (the dashboard showing zero sales for one region two days after launch), naming which environment you would check first and what you would tell the regional manager while still investigating.
slots.deliverable: The six capstone artifacts from the lesson's checklist: user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a written production-incident response.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can explain how Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, and Kanban actually organize real IT work, trace a change through the Dev-QA-UAT-Production release chain, and use Git and a release checklist to describe how software ships safely -- the shared professional foundation every later course in this path assumes.
